blogs.title: Multiphasic Anaphylaxis at the Bedside: When to Move From Repeat IM to an IV Epinephrine Infusion
blogs.description: This post dissects the clinical fork in the road highlighted by the case: repeated intramuscular epinephrine for recurring episodes versus initiating a continuous IV epinephrine infusion. We review operational definitions (biphasic vs refractory vs protracted), practical triggers to escalate (eg, recurrent hypotension/hypoxemia after ≥2 IM doses, oral long‑acting/ongoing absorption, suspected mast cell disease), and safety considerations for IV infusions (telemetry, nurse-driven titration, avoid push-dose boluses). A simple, team-friendly algorithm is offered to reduce delay and anchoring when multiphasic patterns emerge.

blogs.title: 0.5 mg or Bust: Fixing Adult Epinephrine Underdosing in Anaphylaxis
blogs.description: Many adults still receive 0.3 mg IM epinephrine by habit or auto-injector availability, despite guideline dosing of 0.01 mg/kg (max 0.5 mg) and mounting data that underdosing leads to more rescue dosing and escalation (including the 2025 retrospective study cited in the case report). We outline a practical pathway to default 0.5 mg IM for adults >50 kg, reconcile human‑factors advantages of auto-injectors with dose accuracy, and offer QI tactics: stock 0.5 mg options where available, prefilled 0.5 mg syringes, order‑set defaults, and nurse-initiated protocols. The goal: faster first dose, right dose, fewer relapses.

blogs.title: Steroids in Anaphylaxis: Time to Break the Habit
blogs.description: Despite tradition, contemporary evidence shows corticosteroids do not prevent biphasic anaphylaxis and may increase adverse outcomes (eg, higher admission rates), yet they continue to be given—sometimes in duplicative regimens, as in the case. We summarize the data behind guideline shifts away from routine steroids, highlight potential harms (hyperglycemia in diabetics, mood changes, infection), and define the limited scenarios where they may still play a role (eg, coexisting asthma exacerbation)—always as adjuncts, never at the expense of prompt epinephrine.

blogs.title: Tryptase, the 20%+2 Rule, and the Patient You Might Be Missing: Unmasking Mast Cell Disease After Anaphylaxis
blogs.description: Make tryptase part of the anaphylaxis bundle: obtain samples ASAP (without delaying care), again at 1–2 hours (peak), and a baseline ≥24 hours after resolution. We review interpretation using the 1.2×baseline + 2 ng/mL (20%+2) rule to confirm mast‑cell activation and discuss what an elevated baseline suggests (systemic mastocytosis, hereditary alpha‑tryptasemia). The post walks through referral and workup (KIT D816V testing, marrow when appropriate) and the implications for long‑term management: higher‑dose autoinjectors, daily H1/H2 blockade, and consideration of adjuncts like omalizumab in select cases.

blogs.title: The Penicillin Allergy Label That Backfired: How Delabeling Prevents Harm
blogs.description: This case underscores how an unverified, remote penicillin ‘allergy’ can cascade into second‑line prescribing and unexpected harm—here, a severe macrolide anaphylaxis. We propose a fast, safe approach to beta‑lactam allergy evaluation: history‑based risk stratification, direct oral challenge for low‑risk histories, and informed cephalosporin use by side‑chain. Embedding delabeling pathways into ED/inpatient care improves antimicrobial stewardship and likely reduces adverse drug reactions long‑term.

blogs.title: Watching and Waiting: A Pragmatic, Risk‑Stratified Observation Plan After Anaphylaxis
blogs.description: How long should we observe? We translate risk factors into a workable disposition plan: low risk (rapid complete recovery after a single IM dose, known/removed trigger, no high‑risk comorbidity) can be observed 2–4 hours; intermediate risk (unknown trigger, second IM dose, mild comorbidity) merits 6–12 hours; high risk (shock/hypoxemia, multiple doses, delayed epinephrine, oral/long‑acting trigger, suspected mast cell disease, previous biphasic reaction, night‑time events, remote living) warrants 12–24 hours and often admission/ICU monitoring. Discharge essentials include two autoinjectors, a written action plan, and early allergy follow‑up.
